papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention: A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.concept: LLM safety alignment, decomposed into a Harm Detection Direction (harmfulness of a prompt) and a Refusal Execution Direction (the act of refusing).
papers.estimator: First right singular vector of the SVD of a difference-of-activations matrix (harmful minus benign/neutral prompts) at a layer, purified by classifier-guided sparsification: a linear classifier is trained on the same activations, per-neuron importance is taken as the absolute weight |w_j|, a binary mask keeps only neurons above a k-th-percentile importance threshold, and the raw SVD vector is masked and L2-normalized; done separately for the refusal-execution vector (twin benign/harmful prompt pairs) and the harm-detection vector (harmful vs. neutral prompts).
papers.groups: Three harmful-prompt benchmarks used as source datasets for the harm/refusal concept: AdvBench, HarmBench and StrongREJECT (one serves as the calibration set the direction is fit on, the others as unseen test sets); also the official vs. simplified chat-prompt template as a secondary group. papers.estimator: a weighted combination of the top-k PCA components (weighted by their explained-variance ratio) of few-shot activation vectors extracted from a REINFORCE-selected subset of attention heads (mu_ARM = sum w_i * v_i, Sec. 3.3), injected into those heads' outputs at inference to steer the model's judgment
papers.groups: the paper's own preference-criterion splits, each with its own Activation RM built by the same procedure: RewardBench's Chat/Chat Hard/Safety/Reasoning splits, Multimodal RewardBench's Correctness/Preference/Knowledge/Math/Coding/Safety/VQA splits, and PreferenceHack's Length/Format/Positivity bias splits (language-only and multimodal variants)

B.w: Looked in Sec. 3.4 and Sec. 6 for a classification accuracy obtained by projecting held-out items' unmodified activations onto mu_ARM or a probe; the paper's only accuracy numbers (Tables 1-2) require the full causal intervention (injecting mu_ARM into the selected heads, Eq. 1) before the model's own generated token probability is read out, so they are scored under C rather than as a direction-projection/probe classification.

C.q: Across all splits, our Activation Reward Model outperforms all zeroshot and few-shot open-source baselines on both language-only and multimodal benchmarks, closing the gap with GPT-4o.

papers.title: Beyond Task-Level Context: Class-Conditional Context Vectors for Implicit In-Context Learning
papers.concept: the label space of each of nine text-classification tasks (SST-2/SST-5/MR sentiment, TREC question type, AGNews/DBPedia topic, Subj subjectivity, EmoC emotion, HateSpeech18 hate speech); each class within each task (e.g. positive/negative, happy/sad/angry/others) is treated as its own separately-estimated target, not a shared concept
papers.estimator: class-conditional context vector d_c = {mean attention output, mean MLP output} at the end-of-sequence token position across layers, averaged over five labeled demonstrations sampled for class c (a class-mean activation vector), jointly injected into the residual stream with learnable per-layer scaling coefficients trained by gradient descent (cross-entropy) on the same demonstrations
papers.groups: none in the rubric's sense: the nine benchmark datasets are nine different classification concepts (not groups of one shared concept), and within each dataset the classes (e.g. SST-2's positive/negative) are themselves separately-estimated targets rather than data-source/category/topic/template/language subsets of one concept; no single concept's items are ever split into such groups

A.q: In our experiments, Xc consists of the class-conditional context vectors for class c obtained from multiple independent runs with different random seeds.
A.w: Sec. 4.3.2 and Appendix B.2 (Eq. 10): for each class, the context vector d_c is independently refit from five different random seeds (each a different sample of demonstrations, Sec. 4.1), and intra-class distance reports the pairwise cosine distance among these five refits, with results shown per dataset in Figure 3a-b (and Figs. 10-14 for other models).

B.w: Searched Sec. 3.4 and Sec. 4 for an accuracy/AUROC/F1 computed by directly projecting held-out items onto d_c or a linear probe; classification instead always requires a full forward pass with all class-conditional vectors additively injected (Eq. 3-4, 7) and reading off label-token probabilities, which is an intervention-based (steering-style) evaluation rather than a projection/probe classifier, so it is scored under C instead.

C.q: These class-conditional context vectors are additively injected into the model's residual streams in a single forward pass, enabling contextual contributions to be modulated in a class-aware manner while keeping the backbone frozen.
C.w: Abstract and Eq. 3-4 (injection mechanism); Table 1 reports the resulting classification accuracy on a held-out 500-item test set per dataset (LLaMA2-7B), with Tables 6-10 for five further models.

D.q: C3 V outperforms the strongest baseline I2CL by 1.2 points on average, with gains on challenging datasets such as SST-5, HateS, and DBPedia.
D.w: Table 1 (and Tables 6-10) report classification accuracy separately per dataset/task, but each dataset is a different classification concept (sentiment vs. topic vs. hate speech vs. emotion, etc.) rather than the same concept's own data groups, matching D's partial case of comparisons between different concepts' results rather than groups of one concept.

papers.title: DPN-LE: Dual Personality Neuron Localization and Editing for Large Language Models
papers.concept: Big Five personality traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism), each represented as a high-trait vs. low-trait direction, i.e. a persona trait in the survey's sense
papers.estimator: layer-wise steering vector s_l = mean MLP hidden-state (last-token, post-gated-activation) over high-trait contrastive samples minus the same over low-trait samples (Eq. 1, a difference-of-means direction), then sparsified by dual-criterion neuron selection (Cohen's d effect-size threshold and an activation-magnitude quantile threshold, Sec. 4.2) to isolate a mutually-exclusive trait-specific neuron subset
papers.groups: for a given trait concept, the two evaluation instruments the fitted direction/intervention is assessed on: PersonalityBench (the dataset the steering vector is constructed and mainly evaluated on, Table 2) and IPIP-NEO-300 (a separate multiple-choice personality questionnaire used only for a held-out generalization check, Table 5); the five Big Five traits themselves are different concepts, not groups of one another, and LLaMA-3-8B vs. Qwen2.5-7B are different models, also excluded from 'groups'

The steering vector is built once from a fixed, sequentially-selected set of 1,000 question pairs (Appendix C.1), and the 'var' columns in Tables 2/6 are the variance of the GPT-4o trait rating across generated evaluation responses, not spread across resampled fits of the direction.

papers.title: Can Linear Probes Effectively Measure LLM Uncertainty ?
papers.concept: correctness / truthfulness of the LLM's answer, used as a proxy target for factual uncertainty quantification

problems.name: Directions that do not survive a change of data
problems.plain: A detector or steering direction learned on one set of examples often stops working, or quietly gets worse, when the wording, topic, length, format or number of conversation turns changes. Nobody can yet say in advance which changes it will survive.
problems.technical: Probes and steering vectors fit on one prompt distribution degrade under dataset, domain, template, negation, synthetic-to-natural, single-to-multi-turn and short-form-to-long-form generation shifts. The held-out accuracy that papers report does not by itself show robustness to these shifts.

problems.name: The direction may track a proxy, not the concept
problems.plain: A direction built by contrasting two sets of examples picks up every difference between the sets, such as vocabulary, style, topic or difficulty. So a detector that works may be reading the wrong thing.
problems.technical: Difference-of-means and probe directions absorb confounds of the contrast set, including lexical cues, style, topic, length, base rates and the labeler's proxy. Decoding or steering success therefore does not fix what the direction means, and controls that remove the cue often collapse the separation.

problems.name: One straight line may not fit the concept
problems.plain: These methods assume a concept is a single dial inside the model. Many concepts look more like several dials, a curved surface or a region, so one direction captures only part of the concept.
problems.technical: The single-direction linear representation assumption fails for multi-dimensional, multi-valued, curved or nonlinearly encoded concepts. A concept and its opposite can span a subspace rather than sit at opposite ends of one axis, and rank-one task vectors provably fail on general bijections.

problems.name: No ground truth to score against
problems.plain: For most concepts there is no answer key saying what the model really represents. So researchers grade directions with AI judges, proxy scores or best-case numbers, and these can mislead.
problems.technical: Evaluation lacks ground-truth concepts and labels. LLM judges are prompt-sensitive and disagree with humans, best-of-grid and single-number metrics overstate effects, and steering is often not compared with prompting or fine-tuning, which frequently beat it.

problems.name: Readable is not the same as used or steerable
problems.plain: Being able to read a concept out of a model's internals does not mean the model uses it. Being able to push the model with a direction does not mean that direction is how the model actually works.
problems.technical: Probe decodability, causal use and steerability come apart. Decodable directions can have no causal effect, probe accuracy fails to predict steering success, steering can work without decodability, and a direction can be shown sufficient without being shown necessary.

problems.name: The estimated direction is not a unique, stable object
problems.plain: If you rebuild the same concept direction from a different sample, seed, dataset or method, you can get a different arrow that works just as well. So a single reported direction may be neither reproducible nor meaningful on its own.
problems.technical: Directions are non-identifiable. Many distinct or orthogonal directions give equal probe accuracy or steering effect, SAE features are identifiable only up to signed permutation and differ across seeds, estimates from few contrast pairs have high variance, conclusions depend on the estimator, preprocessing and normalization, and directions rotate under fine-tuning.

problems.name: Pushing one thing moves others
problems.plain: Steering a model along one direction also changes things you did not aim at, such as fluency, other traits, general skills or safety. Sometimes these changes are in places nobody checked.
problems.technical: Directions are entangled with other concepts and with capability and safety directions. Steering causes off-target concept shifts, loss of coherence and capability, over-refusal and weaker refusal (even with random or benign vectors), and orthogonalizing the directions does not stop the behavioural spillover.

problems.name: One direction for every input and every group
problems.plain: A single averaged direction is applied to every input, but the concept can point a different way in different contexts, personas, subtypes or groups. The same arrow can then help some cases, do nothing for others and push some the wrong way.
problems.technical: Concept directions rotate with context, persona, prompt format and subtype. A pooled difference of means averages over heterogeneous or multimodal clusters, aggregate success hides reversals at the level of items and slices (anti-steerable inputs, below-chance transfer across subtypes), and static vectors cannot condition on the input.

problems.name: Safety uses break under attack, and removal is shallow
problems.plain: Detectors built on directions can be dodged, safety directions can be cut out to jailbreak a model, and removing a concept usually just hides it where it can still be recovered.
problems.technical: Probes are evaded by models trained or prompted against them, and refusal or safety directions can be removed by ablation and editing attacks. Erasure and unlearning leave the concept recoverable, and steering itself can be a covert attack or be resisted by the model.

problems.name: Directions that do not carry across models, languages or modalities
problems.plain: A direction or steering recipe that works on one model often fails, weakens or even flips on another model, size, language or input type, and nobody can explain why.
problems.technical: Directions, best layers and signal polarity are specific to the model, family, scale and modality. Steering vectors transfer across models only in specific cases, cross-lingual transfer is uneven, and effects can reverse with scale.

problems.name: Sparse features and neurons are shaky building blocks
problems.plain: Tools that split a model's activity into many small features, or into single neurons, are meant to give clean handles on concepts. But the features often mix concepts, miss cases and depend on how the tool was trained, and they rarely beat simpler methods.
problems.technical: SAE latents suffer from absorption, splitting, polysemanticity, frequency bias and reconstruction error. SAE-based probes and steering often do not beat difference-of-means or linear probes, pretrained SAEs exist only for some models and layers, and single neurons are unreliable under superposition.

problems.name: No account of why directions exist or why steering works
problems.plain: We can find and use these directions, but we do not know how the model builds them, why some concepts get one and others do not, or why steering works in some cases and fails in others.
problems.technical: Several things remain unexplained. These include where linear directions come from (learned, or inherited from input statistics), how they are computed and propagate through layers and attention, and which concepts can be steered. Theoretical guarantees for steering are also missing, and the theory that exists holds only in toy or linear-attention settings.

problems.name: Needs inside access, and can only surface what is already there
problems.plain: These methods need to look inside the model, so they cannot be used on closed commercial models. Steering can also only amplify what the model already knows, not add new knowledge or skills.
problems.technical: Direction methods need white-box access to activations, which rules out closed and API-only models. Activation editing only re-weights representations the model already has, so it cannot inject missing knowledge or serve as a standalone or durable safeguard.

problems.name: Steering several things at once
problems.plain: Turning two or more concept dials at the same time often makes them interfere, so steering for several goals together is unreliable.
problems.technical: Composing several steering vectors suffers destructive interference from correlated, non-orthogonal directions. Other obstacles are capacity limits on the safe strength per concept, nonlinear interactions during generation, and a combinatorial number of attribute combinations with little data where the attributes occur together.

problems.name: Choosing layer, strength and token position
problems.plain: Results depend heavily on where in the model you read or push, how hard you push and at which word. These choices are still made by trial and error for every model.
problems.technical: Layer, coefficient, token position, pooling and subspace size are chosen by grid search for each model. Effects are non-monotonic in strength, can reverse when the push is too strong and flip sign across layers, and probe accuracy is a poor guide to where to intervene.

plain.paper_says: The paper builds Latent Guard, a cheap filter that reads the model's own internal sense of whether a request is harmful. Its abstract says this filter does as well as or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a separate model trained only to screen requests, across different jailbreak methods, and the introduction, results and conclusion repeat the claim.
plain.paper_quote: our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods.
plain.paper_quote_where: Abstract, lines 37-39 (the quote runs across line breaks, joined here by single spaces). Repeated at line 1103 ("achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3, a dedicated finetuned model."), in the introduction at lines 159-161 and in the conclusion at lines 1225-1228.
plain.why_wrong: The claim is incomplete rather than false. It holds in most cells of the paper's own Table 3 but fails for one model and one attack type. On Qwen2-7B-Instruct, for jailbreaks that hide a harmful request inside a ready-made prompt template, Latent Guard catches 53.5 percent where Llama Guard 3 catches 91.4 percent, which is neither comparable nor better, and two other cells show smaller shortfalls. The paper does qualify the comparison in Appendix H, but that qualification concerns other datasets and never mentions this cell, and the abstract keeps the unqualified sentence.
plain.evidence: The evidence is the paper's own Table 3, not our measurement. It reports accuracy in percent on prompts that had already got each model to answer instead of refusing. For Qwen2-Instruct-7B, Llama Guard 3 against Latent Guard reads template 91.4 against 53.5, accepted harmful 59.4 against 54.6, persuasion 17.8 against 75.0, adversarial suffix 97.8 against 100.0, and refused harmless 50.0 against 91.6. For Llama3-Instruct-8B the adversarial suffix cell reads 99.2 against 91.0. The caption and the results text say the jailbreak test cases are prompts that successfully jailbreak the model, and the methods section defines template attacks as harmful instructions inserted into carefully constructed jailbreak prompting templates. A reply counts as a refusal only if it contains a stock refusal phrase, so each jailbreak prompt in the test set is one the model answered, and there accuracy is the share of those prompts the filter catches. The paper's own qualification says Latent Guard is worse than Llama Guard 3 on ToxicChat, is poor on the OpenAI Moderation set for Qwen2 and Llama3, can fail on out-of-domain examples, and that the comparison "may be unfair".

plain.headline: A safety probe with a near-perfect score catches only a little over half of the harmful prompts the model would answer
plain.kind: safety monitor or defense misses a category
plain.paper_says: The paper's linear-probe safety monitor reads a direction in Gemma-3-27B-IT's internal activity and flags incoming prompts that score high on it. By the standard pooled measure it separates harmful from harmless prompts almost perfectly, with a harm AUROC of 0.985 (1 would mean every harmful prompt is ranked above every harmless one). Across its six monitors the paper reports 0.945 to 0.994, and in the same sentence it adds that the monitors still miss the harmful prompts the model actually answers.
plain.paper_quote: harm AUROC ranges from 0.945 to 0.994, meaning every monitor separates labeled-harmful from benign prompts nearly perfectly by the standard measure, while still missing the harmful prompts Gemma actually answers.
plain.paper_quote_where: P2546.txt lines 222 to 224, Section 4.1
plain.why_wrong: The near-perfect score is correct as a measure of telling harmful from harmless prompts, but it is misleading as a measure of protection. It averages over all harmful prompts, and it breaks down for one group, the harmful prompts the model would answer, which are the only ones where a catch prevents anything. The probe is set so that it wrongly flags 1 in 100 harmless prompts. At that setting it catches 0.565 of that group against 0.889 of the prompts the model refuses on its own anyway. The paper makes this gap its central result and says the pooled number overstates the protection. So the pooled claim is incomplete, not false, and the paper qualifies it itself.
plain.evidence: This is the paper's own evidence. On Gemma-3-27B-IT the linear probe is set to a 1 percent false-positive rate on a pool of 10,000 harmless WildChat prompts. A prompt counts as one the model would answer if the model complied at least once in eight samples at temperature 1. Recall, the share of harmful prompts caught, is 0.565 on the 138 prompts the model would answer and 0.889 on the 576 it always refused. The gap is 0.324 [95% CI 0.24, 0.41]. The risk ratio is 4.32 [3.2, 6.0], so a prompt the probe misses is 4.32 times as likely to be complied with as one it catches. Harm AUROC is 0.985. Linear probes on two other models show the same pattern. On Qwen3-32B recall is 0.458 against 0.835 (gap 0.377) with 83/631 prompts in the two groups, and on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it is 0.621 against 0.920 (gap 0.298) with 103/611. On Gemma the gap runs from 0.217 to 0.325 across all six monitor configurations, while harm AUROC runs from 0.945 to 0.994. The abstract's range of 0.22 to 0.38 covers those six configurations plus the Qwen3 and Llama probes. The survey gives the Gemma values in its harm table and text.

plain.harm: A team that picked or tuned this probe by its near-perfect pooled score would think it was well protected, yet it would catch only 0.565 of the harmful prompts the model would answer at least some of the time, and a prompt it let through would be 4.32 times as likely to be answered as one it stopped, with nothing in the single score to show this.

"Would answer" means the model complied in at least one of eight samples at temperature 1, as judged by an LLM grader (Claude Opus). The grader declined to judge 13 percent of responses. The paper counts those as not complied and says this can only understate the gap (lines 119 to 122). Because "would answer" means at least one compliance in eight tries, a missed prompt need not come back answered, and the 4.32 is a relative risk, not a count of harmful answers. Only input-side monitors were tested, and the paper says output classifiers "may or may not share the failure" (line 302), so a check placed after the model could still stop some of these answers. The scope is English, single-turn, naturally phrased prompts with no jailbreaks (line 300). The paper notes that such probes are now deployed in production systems (line 73) but reports no incident, so this is what would follow for a user of the pooled number, not a documented harm. The source is a single-author arXiv preprint (2609.05797v1, 5 Sep 2026) submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 JUDGe Workshop (line 50), with no sign of completed review. Flag for the authors, not edited here. harm.tex lines 132 to 133 introduce this case as a monitor missing a whole category of harm, a language or a modality. The group here is none of those. It is set by the model's own behaviour, the prompts it would answer.

plain.headline: A harmful-request filter that tests at 99.4 percent would flag 0.0 percent of HarmBench's harmful requests
plain.kind: false safety assurance, a safety monitor misses a whole benchmark from a source it never saw (source, not a hidden subgroup)
plain.caveat: The paper reports this collapse itself as the result that motivates its study, and its title is "False Sense of Security". So the paper does not leave the in-distribution claim standing, and the harm falls on anyone who trusts an in-distribution score of the kind the paper says prior work reported. The requests the probe misses make up a whole benchmark from another source, not a subgroup hidden inside a pooled score, so this is a failure to transfer. The 0.0 is the worst cell in Table 1. The same probe flags 1.2 percent of AdvBench, and the same model's BeaverTailsEval probe flags 16.5 percent of HarmBench. Still, no probe in Table 1 flags more than 30.5 percent of HarmBench or 43.4 percent of AdvBench. The two numbers measure different things. The 99.4 is accuracy on a mix of benign and harmful requests. The 0.0 is the share of harmful requests flagged on a benchmark that is all harmful. All scores are accuracy at the SVM's own decision rule. The paper reports no ranking score such as AUROC, so it does not show whether a different cutoff would catch some of the missed requests. The size of HarmBench was not read from the source, so the case gives a percentage and not a count. A request the probe misses reaches the model unflagged. Whether the model then answers it depends on the model's own refusals, and this table does not measure that.

plain.kind: safety monitor or defense misses a category
plain.paper_says: The paper uses a probe, a simple classifier that reads a model's internal signals, to tell safe requests from unsafe ones in two vision-language models. It reports that probes trained and tested on text versions of the requests, where each picture is replaced by a written caption, are right about 90 percent of the time at middle layers. It then reports, as its central finding, that the same probes misjudge the original requests with pictures and call most unsafe ones safe.
plain.paper_quote: For both LLaVA-1.5-7B and MiniGPT-4-7B, the binary classifiers trained on the textonly dataset Dtt achieve ∼ 90% accuracy on its test set at middle layers
plain.paper_quote_where: Lines 489-491, Section 4, Observation 1 (the probing results for Figure 3)
plain.why_wrong: Nothing the paper claims is wrong. The 90 percent is measured on text only, and the paper itself shows that it does not carry over. What would fail is a reader's belief that a probe proven on text will also screen requests that come with pictures. It fails on exactly those image-and-text requests. There the text-trained probe falls to about 60 percent at middle layers and calls about 70 percent of the unsafe requests safe. So as a guide to image requests the 90 percent tells only part of the story. It is not false.

Lines 489-491 say that for both LLaVA-1.5-7B and MiniGPT-4-7B, probes trained on the text set reach about 90 percent on its test part at middle layers. Lines 397-401 say about 95 percent of safe and about 70 percent of unsafe image-and-text requests are classified as safe, "suggesting a clear tendency to overestimate the safety of vision-language inputs". Lines 244-245 say the text set is built by replacing each image with its caption. Lines 1667-1674 say the unsafe requests come from MM-SafetyBench, where "the harmful content is embedded within the images" and the text alone is not malicious, and the safe ones come from LLaVA-Instruct-80k. Line 492 says probes trained on the image-and-text inputs reach only about 65 percent, "barely above random guessing". An activation steering method that protects models from

In their words the methods "maintain refusal on standard harmful queries but collapse under adversarial attacks". On Llama-8B the largest gain in utility, 12 percent with LinearProbe, comes with the largest drop in robustness, 55 percent. Plain refusal does slip in a few cases. It drops by 10 percent with LinearProbe on Llama-8B, and by 7 to 8 percent with DiffMeans, LinearProbe and ReFT-r1 on Llama-3B. steering vectors still showing an improvement over

claim.title: Shifting Perspectives: Steering Vectors for Robust Bias Mitigation in LLMs

harm.harm_type: claim of generality left standing

plain.headline: A debiasing paper says both its edits reduce stereotyping on a second bias test, but on that test the linear edit leaves it about where it was
plain.kind: claim of generality left standing
plain.paper_says: The paper (Spectral Editing of Activations for Large Language Model Alignment) shifts a chat model's internal signals to make it less biased, in two versions, a linear edit (Linear-SEA) and a nonlinear one (Phi-SEA). It fits both edits on examples from one bias test, BBQ, then scores them on a second test, CrowS-Pairs, and says both versions reduce bias across most of that test's ten groups.
plain.paper_quote: Results demonstrate that both SEA variants effectively reduce model bias across most categories, with Φ-SEA notably decreasing the generation of stereotypical sentences by 7%.
plain.paper_quote_where: Section 4.6 (Generalisation of Editing Effects to Similar Tasks), lines 1451 to 1452, the sentence summarising Table 5
plain.why_wrong: The sentence is true of Phi-SEA, which lowers 8 of the 10 groups, but not of Linear-SEA, which lowers only 4, leaves 3 unchanged, raises 3 very slightly and leaves the overall figure almost where it was. So the claim is overstated for one of the two versions, not false as a whole. The paper does warn that the linear edit's gain on its main bias test BBQ is modest and mixed, but it does not repeat that warning for CrowS-Pairs.
plain.evidence: This is the paper's own evidence, from its Table 5. Each value is the percent of CrowS-Pairs sentence pairs where the model rates the stereotyped sentence as more likely, so lower is better. The unedited row is labelled only 'LLaMA-2'. The paper's main model elsewhere is LLaMA-2-Chat-7B, and Table 5 does not say so again, so that identity is inferred. The overall figure is 64.16 unedited, 64.10 with Linear-SEA and 57.96 with Phi-SEA. Linear-SEA improves 4 of 10 groups (Age 75.82 to 74.73, Disability 73.85 to 72.31, Nationality 61.11 to 60.19, Appearance 72.22 to 70.83). It leaves 3 unchanged (Autre 72.73, Religion 75.68, Sexual Orientation 86.02) and worsens 3 (Gender 61.56 to 62.19, Race/Color 53.15 to 53.35, Socioeconomic 71.58 to 72.11). Phi-SEA improves 8 of 10, leaves Autre unchanged at 72.73 and worsens Age (75.82 to 78.02). Elsewhere the paper says linear editing 'almost does not hurt the model's other capabilities', while the nonlinear edit shows 'a more visible decrease in common-sense QA'. It also qualifies the linear edit on BBQ, saying its gain there is 'modest, exhibiting a mere increase of 0.78%', and that across models 'linear SEA can marginally improve accuracy, but the other two metrics are mixed'.
plain.evidence_where: runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P1478.txt, Table 5 caption at line 1360 and values at lines 1385 (LLaMA-2 row label) to 1443 (last Phi-SEA value, 57.96), with the unedited average 64.16 at line 1407. The claim is at lines 1451 to 1452. The other-skills remark is at lines 1351 to 1353. The BBQ qualifications are at line 1164 and line 1182. LLaMA-2-Chat-7B as the main model is at line 891 (Figure 3 caption) and line 1446. The case record is id P1478 in SURVEY/work/harm_cases.json, and its omission from the harm table is at line 23 of SURVEY/paper/sections/harm.tex.
plain.harm: A developer who took the Table 5 summary sentence on its own and picked the linear edit, which the paper says spares the model's other skills, would expect it to cut stereotyping on a new bias test and would instead get a model that prefers the stereotyped sentence about as often as before, in 64.16% of pairs unedited and 64.10% after the edit.
plain.caveat: The skeptic rated this case weak, and the survey leaves it out of the harm table (harm.tex line 23). The three groups the linear edit makes worse each rise by less than one point (Gender 61.56 to 62.19, Race/Color 53.15 to 53.35, Socioeconomic 71.58 to 72.11), and Table 5 reports no spread or significance test, so these are slight drift and not a model made measurably worse. The harm is false reassurance, not damage. It also falls only on a reader who trusts the summary sentence alone, because the paper warns in its main bias results that the linear edit's gain on BBQ is modest (line 1164) and that its other bias metrics across models are mixed (line 1182). The other version, Phi-SEA, does lower the overall figure from 64.16 to 57.96, and the sentence's own number is about that version, though Phi-SEA pushes Age the wrong way (75.82 to 78.02). What fails is a whole method version, not one group hidden inside a pooled fit.

claim.title: Spectral Editing of Activations for Large Language Model Alignment

harm.harm_type: decision carried to the wrong model or setting

plain.headline: A truthfulness edit makes a chat model pick the true answer less often on three fact-checking tests
plain.kind: decision carried to the wrong model or setting
plain.paper_says: The TruthX paper calls ITI one of the state-of-the-art methods for making a language model more truthful by editing its internal representations. ITI learns a direction inside the model's attention heads and nudges the model along it. The paper spells out the setup (train on TruthfulQA, then test on other benchmarks) only for its own method TruthX. Of ITI it says only that all methods follow the standard TruthfulQA settings.
plain.paper_quote: The state-of-the-art methods for enhancing LLM’s truthfulness through editing internal representations, including ContrastConsistent Search (CCS) (Burns et al., 2023), Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) (Li et al., 2023b)
plain.paper_quote_where: P0156.txt lines 551-555, Baselines section (the Representation Editing entry). The sentence goes on at line 556 with "all learn a direction within attention heads and accordingly edit attention patterns of LLM."
plain.why_wrong: The "enhancing truthfulness" label holds on Natural Questions, where the ITI model scores higher than the unedited model. It fails on all three FACTOR fact-checking sets, where the ITI model picks the true answer less often than the unedited one. In plain terms, the edit meant to make the model more truthful makes it choose a false option more often on these tests. The paper prints these drops in its own Table 2, never discusses them, and makes its claim about carrying over to new benchmarks only for TruthX. So calling ITI a truthfulness gain is incomplete rather than false. It is a failure to carry over to benchmarks ITI was not built on, not a group hidden inside ITI's own test.
plain.evidence: This is the paper's own table (Table 2, Llama-2-7B-Chat, multiple-choice accuracy with no outside documents). The ITI numbers are the TruthX authors' replications, made from ITI's publicly available models and outputs. Going from the unedited model to ITI, Natural Questions rises from 54.90 to 57.83 and TriviaQA falls from 66.75 to 65.95. FACTOR news falls from 64.67 to 53.28, FACTOR expert from 64.83 to 51.69 and FACTOR wiki from 56.95 to 43.82. For comparison TruthX gets 59.60 on Natural Questions, 66.79 on TriviaQA, 65.83 on news, 65.25 on expert and 57.18 on wiki. The paper says the TruthX model trained on TruthfulQA is applied directly to these benchmarks to test how well it carries over to new kinds of questions. It says all benchmarks are scored as multiple-choice accuracy in a closed-book setting, and that all methods apply the standard settings of TruthfulQA. The generalization paragraph discusses only TruthX ("TruthX exhibits stronger generalization among various domains") and says nothing about the ITI drops. No uncertainty or test-set size is reported for these accuracies.
plain.evidence_where: All in runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P0156.txt. Table 2 values at lines 703-736, caption at lines 738-740. TruthX-only setup (trained on TruthfulQA, applied to other benchmarks) at lines 533-535. Multiple-choice, closed-book scoring at lines 536-537. ITI described as a state-of-the-art truthfulness method at lines 551-556, and again at line 745. "All methods apply the standard settings of TruthfulQA" at line 558. plain.harm: A developer who added ITI to a chat model to make it more truthful, and checked it only on a general question-answering test such as Natural Questions where it scores higher, would end up with a model that picks the true answer less often than the unedited model on the three FACTOR fact-checking test sets (the paper labels them news, expert and wiki).
plain.caveat: The ITI numbers come from a competing paper's replication, built from ITI's public models and outputs, on one model, and the paper gives no ITI settings. So the drop may partly reflect how ITI was run and not ITI itself. The quoted description of ITI is the TruthX authors' wording, not a claim made by the ITI paper. The paper states the train-on-TruthfulQA, test-elsewhere setup explicitly only for TruthX. For ITI it says only that all methods follow the standard TruthfulQA settings. All these tests are multiple choice, so they show the edited model choosing a false option more often, not writing false answers in free text. The weak results are on whole benchmarks ITI was not built on. So this is a failure to carry over to new settings, not a group hidden inside its own test. No uncertainty or test-set size is reported for these accuracies. The case was rated moderate and left out of the paper's harm table.

claim.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model

plain.headline: A hallucination detector said to generalize across sentence forms is little better than guessing on "or" sentences
plain.kind: claim of generality left standing
plain.paper_says: The paper trains its PRISM hallucination detector only on plain affirmative statements. It then says the detector "achieves significant generalization performance across different grammatical structures", meaning statements with "not", with "and" and with "or", and it names no structure as an exception.
plain.paper_quote: However, our framework achieves significant generalization performance across different grammatical structures.
plain.paper_quote_where: Line 1092, in the Experiment section's discussion of Table 5 (LogicStruct dataset)
plain.why_wrong: The claim holds on average and for sentences joined by "and". It fails for sentences joined by "or", where both PRISM versions on both models score 0.5329 to 0.6207 in accuracy on sets that are half true and half false, so guessing would be right about half the time. The mass-mean version (PRISM-MM) is also near guessing on "not" sentences. The paper prints these numbers in its own Table 5 but never qualifies the sentence, so the claim is incomplete rather than false. Read as a comparison with the baselines, it still fails on "or" sentences, where the LN-PP baseline beats three of the four PRISM scores.
plain.evidence: Every number comes from the paper's own Table 5. That table covers the LogicStruct dataset, with the detector trained only on affirmative statements, and reports accuracy on negated / conjunction / disjunction statements. PRISM-MM scores 0.5548 / 0.8087 / 0.5580 on LLaMA2-7B-Chat and 0.5260 / 0.8734 / 0.6207 on LLaMA2-13B-Chat. PRISM-SAPLMA scores 0.7345 / 0.7529 / 0.5329 on 7B and 0.7389 / 0.8112 / 0.5722 on 13B. So all four disjunction scores fall between 0.5329 and 0.6207, against 0.7529 to 0.8734 on conjunctions. Guessing would be right about half the time, because the paper balances true and false statements within each grammatical structure and within the disjunction set by construction. Averaged over the three structures PRISM scores 0.6405 to 0.7074, above every baseline average (the highest is 0.5710), and that is the sense in which the sentence holds. On disjunctions alone the LN-PP baseline, which does not use PRISM's prompt, scores 0.5743 (7B) and 0.5863 (13B). That is above every PRISM disjunction score except PRISM-MM on 13B at 0.6207. The plain MM baseline scores 0.4948 (7B) and 0.5071 (13B) on negated statements, so PRISM-MM gains little over it on "not" sentences.

plain.caveat: The paper prints the failing numbers in its own Table 5. The sentence also follows a comparison with baselines that mostly sit near chance, so part of the claim is relative, and on average PRISM does beat every baseline. harm.harm_type: claim of generality left standing

plain.headline: A "task-agnostic" truth reader is near a coin flip on two of its ten tasks on UnifiedQA, and on one of them a reader trained with the answers gets 89 percent right
plain.kind: claim of generality left standing
plain.paper_says: The paper presents CCS, a way to find a truth signal inside a language model's internal activity without being shown any right answers. It argues that this signal is not tied to one task, because it carries over between ten quite different kinds of yes-no question. The section making the point is headed "CCS finds a task-agnostic representation of truth", though its body only says transfer works "in the majority of datasets" and that models "may" hold such a representation.

plain.why_wrong: The heading holds on average but fails on two of the ten tasks. On UnifiedQA, CCS scores 56 on QNLI and 54 on PIQA, where guessing scores 50, and it scores that low even when trained on those very tasks, while a simple reader trained with the right answers on the same model's internals scores 89 on QNLI and 71 on PIQA. So the claim is incomplete rather than false. The body hedges it ("in the majority of datasets", "may"), and the paper's measured claim, that transfer rivals training on the same task, still holds on these two tasks, so what fails is the heading's unqualified "task-agnostic".
plain.evidence: All numbers come from the paper's own figures and tables. Only the assignment of one unlabeled figure block to UnifiedQA is our reading. The labels are balanced (line 312), so guessing scores 50. CCS is the paper's method for finding a truth signal in a model's internals without right answers. UnifiedQA (UQA) is one of its six models. In main-text Figure 2, whose UQA panel is labelled at line 510, the "No Transfer" row (CCS trained and tested on the same task, line 540) reads 94 96 92 99 88 64 89 56 54 89. The columns are IMDB, Amazon, AG News, DBpedia, COPA, RTE, BoolQ, QNLI, PIQA and Story Cloze (label row line 548). So QNLI gets 56 and PIQA 54, against 94, 96, 92 and 99 on the sentiment and topic tasks. Training on another task does not rescue them. The best transfer into QNLI is 64 (from IMDB, line 513) and the best into PIQA is 63 (from Amazon, COPA and Story Cloze, lines 514, 526 and 535). RTE, the other inference task, is not near chance. It gets 64 with no transfer and 75 when CCS is trained on BoolQ (line 529). The same rows appear in the UQA block of Figure 9 (lines 1608 to 1626). Table 1, which averages over all prompts and datasets (caption line 388), gives CCS on UQA 82.1 (line 370). That equals the mean of the ten numbers in the No Transfer row, so the two weak tasks are blended into the summary figure. Table 1 also gives UQA 89.8 for logistic regression (line 372). This is a simple reader trained with the right answers, and the paper treats it as a ceiling (line 323). Its per-task numbers are in Figure 9's LR panel (label line 1715, caption line 1957), whose blocks carry no model names in the text layer. We read the block at lines 1777 to 1787 as UQA because the blocks run TPC, BSS, LR for each model and their No Transfer rows match the tables. By our arithmetic the UQA rows average 78.8, 80.0 and 89.9 (lines 1763, 1775, 1787), against Table 2's 78.8 and 80.0 (lines 766 to 767) and Table 1's 89.8. The T5 blocks just before average 68.3, 67.3 and 84.7 (lines 1727, 1739, 1751), against 68.3 and 67.4 (lines 760 to 761) and 84.6 (line 365). CCS is near chance on QNLI and PIQA even when trained on them, so this is not a direction failing on a group it was never fitted on. The paper's measured claim, that transfer is competitive with no transfer, holds here, since transfer into QNLI and PIQA beats no transfer (64 against 56, 63 against 54). What fails is the unhedged heading. claim.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

harm.harm_type: wrong scientific conclusion

plain.paper_says: The paper recounts that a classifier trained on the model's internal activations for plain sentences without "not" (affirmative statements, such as "The city of Bhopal is in India") reached high accuracy at telling true from false, which "suggested that LLMs internally represent the truthfulness of statements" (Azaria and Mitchell 2023). It also reports that its own direction tA, fitted the same way on affirmative statements only, separates true and false affirmative statements across topics, and says in the same sentence that this direction fails on negated statements.
plain.paper_quote: The resulting classifier achieved high accuracy in determining whether a given statement is true or false. This suggested that LLMs internally represent the truthfulness of statements.
plain.paper_quote_where: P1482.txt lines 59 to 61. The sentence runs over two line breaks in the text file ("accuracy" / "in determining", "internally" / "represent"), shown here as single spaces. The paper is recounting the conclusion drawn from Azaria and Mitchell 2023, which it goes on to correct, not endorsing it.
plain.why_wrong: The conclusion holds only for the sentence form the detector was fitted and tested on, and the paper itself shows that its own affirmative-only direction tA does not accurately separate true from false sentences with "not", such as "The Spanish word 'dos' does not mean 'enemy'", because tA is a mix of the general truth signal tG and a second signal tP that flips sign when "not" is added. So the claim is incomplete rather than false, since tA does carry part of the general signal and works on affirmative sentences, and the failure is on a sentence form that was never in the original training or testing, not a group hidden inside a reported average.
plain.evidence: The evidence is the paper's own and it is mostly shown in figures. Its direction tA is fitted on affirmative statements only, using the instruction-tuned LLaMA3-8B model at layer 12. The text says true and false affirmative statements separate along tA "with a small overlap". It also says tA "does not accurately separate true and false negated statements", because tA "is a linear combination of tG and tP". The Figure 1 caption says "negated true and false statements do not separate along tA". The Figure 5 caption says a direction trained on affirmative statements about cities generalises to affirmative scientific facts "but not to negated statements". The text gives no number for tA on negated statements. For comparison, the paper's fix tG separates an equal mix of affirmative and negated statements with AUROC 0.98. AUROC is a score where 1 means true and false are sorted perfectly, 0.5 means chance and 0 means sorted in reverse. The second direction tP scores close to one on affirmative and close to zero on negated statements. That reversal is what tP is built to do, so it is not the failure. The failure of the Azaria and Mitchell classifier itself is another paper's result that this paper only recounts. That classifier is a multilayer perceptron (a small neural network) trained only on affirmative statements, and Levinstein and Herrmann showed it "fails to generalise in a basic way, namely from affirmative to negated statements". The case is rated weak in the survey's case file.
plain.evidence_where: runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P1482.txt. Model is LLaMA3-8B instruct, line 138. Layer 12, line 243. tA fitted on affirmative statements only, lines 265 to 266. tA separates affirmative with a small overlap but not negated, and is a linear combination of tG and tP, lines 267 to 269 (also lines 101 to 103). Figure 1 caption, lines 119 to 120. Figure 5 left panel caption, lines 427 to 429. tG AUROC 0.98 on an equal mix of affirmative and negated statements, lines 259 to 264. tP AUROC close to one on affirmative and close to zero on negated, lines 318 to 321. Azaria and Mitchell classifier is an MLP, line 55. It was trained only on affirmative statements, lines 70 to 71. Levinstein and Herrmann's result as recounted, lines 75 to 77. Marks and Tegmark's result as recounted, lines 78 to 83. Example sentences, line 172 (Bhopal) and line 200 ('dos'). Weak rating, SURVEY/work/harm_cases.json entry P1482 field strength.
plain.harm: Anyone who trusted a lie detector that reads true or false from a model's internal state and was checked only on sentences without "not" would get unreliable verdicts on sentences with "not", and would wrongly conclude it had found the model's general sense of truth, with nothing in the original tests to warn them.
plain.headline: A lie detector checked only on sentences without "not" would fail to tell true from false once "not" is added
plain.kind: wrong scientific conclusion
plain.caveat: Earlier work had already reported this failure (Levinstein and Herrmann, and Marks and Tegmark, lines 75 to 83). This paper explains why it happens and offers a fix, the direction tG, trained on both sentence forms, which separates both. The failure of the Azaria and Mitchell classifier is recounted here, not measured. What this paper does measure is its own affirmative-only direction, and it shows the size of that failure only in Figures 1 and 5, with no number in the text. Sentences with "not" were never part of the original training or testing, so this is a failure on a sentence form nobody tested, not a group hidden inside a reported average. The harm table labels the case "group", and its caption counts a sentence form as a group even when it was left out of the fit. That label should not be read as a hidden subgroup. For these reasons the case is rated weak.

plain.headline: Steering said to transfer especially well to Tamil and Thai leaves both at coin-flip level
plain.kind: wrong scientific conclusion
plain.paper_says: The paper uses English example pairs to find which parts of a model matter for a two-choice reasoning test. It then adjusts those same parts when the model answers the test in eight other languages. It says this transferred especially well to Tamil, Thai and Turkish, that the key parts are shared across languages, and that this supports using the method across languages.
plain.paper_quote: We found that SADI displayed enhanced language transfer capabilities, particularly in Tamil, Thai, and Turkish. These successful interventions suggest that critical elements are shared across languages, supporting SADI’s utility in cross-lingual applications.
plain.paper_quote_where: Appendix A.4 (Cross-lingual SADI), lines 1745-1747, the paragraph under Table 10
plain.why_wrong: The claim is incomplete rather than false. Read as a comparison with the other method in the table, fine-tuning on English, it is literally true, but in Tamil and Thai every method, including no adjustment at all, scores about what guessing scores, and the method looks better only because English fine-tuning drops a little below guessing, so these two languages show no successful intervention and no evidence of a shared mechanism. Turkish is a real gain for one variant of the method, and the paper does not qualify the sentence for the other two.
plain.evidence: The evidence is the paper's own Table 10, which reports test accuracy with the model parts found from English pairs, in the order no adjustment / fine-tuning on English / the method adjusting attention heads / the method adjusting single neurons. Tamil is 49.40 / 47.00 / 50.20 / 49.80. Thai is 50.80 / 49.60 / 51.00 / 51.00. Turkish is 49.40 / 57.80 / 51.20 / 59.60, so the neuron variant does gain there. Each question has a premise and two answers and the test is translated from that English task, so a coin flip scores 50. The three named languages are the ones where the method beats English fine-tuning. In Indonesian (51.40 / 68.60 / 62.80 / 60.40), Italian, Swahili, Vietnamese and Chinese it goes the other way. The paper's Table 8 builds the examples in each target language instead, and Tamil still scores 50.00 / 48.80 / 49.60 under the three variants there, so building Tamil examples does not lift it either (Thai there is 51.20 / 53.80 / 51.40). The paper's dataset-size table lists no test size for this multilingual task, so a gap of a point or so cannot be judged against noise.
plain.evidence_where: runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P1004.txt, Table 10 at lines 1683-1738 (caption 1683-1684, row labels 1691-1696, Indonesian 1685-1689, Tamil 1710-1714, Thai 1716-1720, Turkish 1722-1726, Italian 1698-1702, Swahili 1704-1708, Vietnamese 1728-1732, Chinese 1734-1738); English fine-tuning described at line 1744; claim at lines 1745-1747; two-answer format at line 1502; translation from the English task at line 1527; Table 8 at lines 1019-1089 (Tamil 1067-1069, Thai 1071-1073); Table 9 dataset sizes at lines 1535-1580, with no entry for the multilingual task. Survey text in SURVEY/paper/sections/harm.tex line 59 (table row) and lines 112-117. Case record in SURVEY/work/harm_cases.json under id P1004.
plain.harm: Anyone who trusted this sentence would apply an adjustment built from English examples to Tamil or Thai questions and still get a model that scores about what guessing scores, and a researcher who cited those two languages as evidence of a mechanism shared across languages would be citing languages where the table shows no measurable effect.
plain.caveat: The case is rated weak. The sentence very likely compares the method with English fine-tuning, and as that comparison it holds, since the method edges fine-tuning in Tamil (50.20 vs 47.00), Thai (51.00 vs 49.60) and Turkish (59.60 vs 57.80). What fails is the step from there to successful interventions and a shared mechanism, because in Tamil and Thai no method gets away from guessing. Turkish supports transfer for the neuron variant (59.60 against 49.40 with no adjustment). The paper gives no test size for this task, so small gaps cannot be judged against noise. The result sits in an appendix. The harm falls on the paper's conclusion and on anyone who builds on it, and it is not a documented harm to any user.

plain.headline: A refusal filter that scores 0.99 across 14 languages would block most harmless Yoruba requests
plain.kind: group hidden by a pooled score (our reading)
plain.paper_says: The dataset's source paper (P1571, Wang et al., "Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages") writes that refusal directions generalize across both high- and low-resource languages, and it lists Yoruba among its mid- and low-resource languages. It qualifies this itself, calling Yoruba safety-misaligned on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B and writing that the refusal direction "is only transferable across safety-aligned languages", and it reports no pooled detection score (the 0.99 in this case is our own number).
plain.paper_quote: refusal directions are not specific to individual languages but generalize effectively across both high-resource and low-resource languages.
plain.paper_quote_where: Section 6 (Exploring the Geometry of Refusal in LLMs), first paragraph, lines 826-827 of the text file. The file has a line break between "generalize" and "effectively". The paper's own qualification is at lines 811-812 ("refusal direction is only transferable across safety-aligned languages", end of Section 5). Yoruba is classed as safety-misaligned at lines 334-337 (Section 4), and listed among mid- and low-resource languages in the footnote at line 607.
plain.why_wrong: At our reading the sentence holds for 13 of the 14 languages but not for Yoruba. A direction fitted on the other 13 ranks a harmful Yoruba request above a harmless one only about 71 times in 100, and Yoruba's own direction points well away from theirs (cosine 0.23, against at least 0.96 for every other language). The paper's own qualification already names Yoruba, so its general sentence is incomplete rather than false. What hides Yoruba is the pooled 0.99, which averages one weak language in with 13 strong ones.
plain.evidence: This is our measurement, status measured. The weak Yoruba reading broke our own registered prediction that every language would read at 0.9 or better (RUNLOG 2026-09-19, PR3 missed). The cutoff rates come from a recalibration run registered before it ran (RUNLOG 2026-09-23). Pooled over all 14 languages and scored on held-out folds, the refusal direction reaches AUROC 0.9926. In plain words it ranks a harmful request above a harmless one about 99 times in 100. With the direction fitted on the other 13 languages, Yoruba reads at 0.7121, against 0.9914 (Arabic) to 0.9999 (English) for every other language, on 128 harmful and 128 harmless prompts per language. Yoruba's own direction reads its held-out half at 0.9684. But its cosine with the direction from the other 13 is only 0.2299, against 0.9605 to 0.9933 for the other languages. In plain words it points a different way. Fitting with Yoruba included barely changes the direction (cosine 0.9998 with the one fitted without it) and lowers the pooled score by only 0.0036. The shared cutoff is set to flag 10 percent of the other languages' harmless prompts. At that cutoff 91.4 percent of harmless Yoruba prompts are flagged and 0 percent of harmful ones are missed. With a cutoff set on labelled Yoruba prompts, false alarms are 12.8 percent and 79.2 percent of harmful Yoruba prompts are missed. At four other model readings Yoruba reads at 0.9206 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), 0.9612 (Qwen2.5-14B), 0.8450 (Llama-3.3-70B) and 0.9093 (Qwen2.5-72B). There the shared cutoff flags 33.6, 28.5, 37.5 and 2.4 percent of harmless Yoruba prompts and misses 6.4, 4.7, 11.3 and 55.5 percent of harmful ones. Label 1 is harmful (checked in the prompt text), and the rates are ordered false alarm then miss (scripts/recalibrate.py).
plain.evidence_where: Pooled 0.9926 is in runs/soundness/blend_in70.json, sets['Refusal, languages'].cv_auroc_all 0.99258. Cosine 0.9998 and the 0.0036 drop are in the same file, groups row set 'Refusal, languages' group lang:yo, cos_with_without 0.99983 and d_cv_auroc -0.00355 (cv_all minus cv_minus, scripts/blend_in70.py line 62). The held-out values 0.7121, own 0.9684, cosine 0.2299, n 128/128, the other languages 0.9914 (ar) to 0.9999 (en) and their cosines 0.9605 (ja) to 0.9933 (nl) are in runs/soundness/loso_detection.json, sets['Refusal, languages'].situations (auroc_loso, auroc_within, cos_loso). Shared and Yoruba-only cutoff rates are in runs/soundness/recal/corpus.json, row polyrefuse_llama3-8b_L16 lang:yo, M0 [0.9141, 0.0] and oracle [0.1282, 0.7922]. Other readings are in runs/soundness/recal/llama31-8b-inst_L13.json (auroc 0.9206, M0 [0.3362, 0.0641]), qwen25-14b_L19.json (0.9612, [0.2853, 0.0472]), llama33-70b_L32.json (0.8450, [0.3748, 0.1125]) and qwen25-72b_L32.json (0.9093, [0.0242, 0.5550]), each row lang:yo. The 10 percent target (FPR 0.10), the rate order and the 50 percent failure line are in scripts/recalibrate.py lines 17, 19 and 64. Labels were checked in runs/external/polyrefuse_llama3-8b_L16.npz (text and y, label 1 on the tax-fraud and hacking prompts). The registered prediction and its miss are in RUNLOG.md around lines 8458 and 8492, and the recalibration registration at line 13407. The paper's qualification is in runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P1571.txt, lines 334-337, 632-633 and 811-812.
plain.harm: Anyone who trusted the pooled 0.99 and ran this direction as one shared refusal filter across the 14 languages would, at this reading, turn away about nine in ten harmless Yoruba requests, and giving Yoruba its own cutoff would instead let about four in five harmful Yoruba requests through.
plain.caveat: This is our own measurement at one model reading (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, layer 16, last token) of the PolyRefuse data, and no real incident happened. The paper tests this model in its English ablation figure but not at our layer and token. The paper that built the dataset does not hide the weakness. It calls Yoruba safety-misaligned and says the refusal direction transfers only across safety-aligned languages, so what hides Yoruba here is the pooled score, not that paper. We test whether the direction can tell harmful from harmless Yoruba prompts, not whether removing it breaks refusal. The paper finds that removing it does raise Yoruba compliance (on gemma-2-9B-it, from around 58 percent to over 90 percent). The Yoruba figures treat Yoruba as a language the filter was not tuned on, because the direction and cutoff are set on the other 13 languages. Adding Yoruba back barely moves the direction. But a cutoff tuned with Yoruba's harmless requests included would sit higher, so the 91 percent describes a filter not tuned on Yoruba. At the four other model readings the direction reads Yoruba far better (0.845 to 0.961) and the damage is smaller. On three of them the shared cutoff flags 28.5 to 37.5 percent of harmless Yoruba requests, about three times the 10 percent it was set for. That is still below the recalibration script's own failure line of 50 percent. On Qwen2.5-72B it misses 55.5 percent of harmful Yoruba requests, which crosses that line. Yoruba has a clear refusal direction of its own (0.968), so a separate Yoruba filter could work. The harm comes from trusting one shared filter because of its pooled score.

plain.headline: A misalignment data screen scoring 0.963 overall flags all secure code, and retuned on code it still lets about half the insecure code through
plain.kind: safety monitor or defense misses a category
plain.paper_says: The dataset's source paper, P1086 from OpenAI, finds that fine-tuning a model on insecure code or on bad advice makes it misbehave on unrelated requests (emergent misalignment), and it proposes auditing fine-tuning data with a feature inside the model, suggesting its toxic-persona feature could be an effective classifier of suspicious training data because that feature rises when as little as 5 percent of a dataset is incorrect. That proposal tracks one feature over a whole dataset on GPT-4o, so the paper makes no claim about the simple sample-by-sample direction on open models that we test.
plain.paper_quote:
The latent increases with as little as 5% incorrect data, suggesting it
could be an effective classifier of potentially suspicious training data.
plain.paper_quote_where: Appendix G, Dataset mixtures and emergent realignment, extended results, lines 2532 to 2533 (the quote runs over the line break). The same proposal is in Section 4, Training on clean data, lines 1051 to 1062.
plain.why_wrong: The idea that one shared pattern in the model can screen this data holds on average but fails for code, the topic where emergent misalignment was first found. Pooled over nine topics, a simple direction built from the paper's released data ranks a bad sample above a good one about 96 times in 100, but on held-out code only about 72 times in 100. A cut-off set on the other topics flags every secure code sample along with every insecure one, and a cut-off retuned on labelled code still misses about half the insecure samples. For the paper's own tool, which we did not test, this shows a gap in the case for screening, not that the tool fails.
plain.evidence: This is our measurement. The per-topic scores come from the corpus's standard leave-one-topic-out test. The cut-off study was registered before it was run (RUNLOG 2026-09-23 20:36), but this case is one row of its output, picked after the results were in. Pooled over 9 topics and 1800 items the direction scores 0.9634. With code held out and the direction fitted on the other eight topics, code scores 0.7173, while the other eight score 0.9716 (Math) to 1.0 (Education). A direction fitted on half the code and tested on the other half reaches only 0.84328. The code group's own direction has cosine 0.274 with the direction pooled from the other topics, against 0.870 to 0.960 for the other topics, so code points a different way. One cut-off, set at 10 percent false alarms on the other topics' aligned items, gives on code a false alarm rate of 1.0 and a miss rate of 0.0. A cut-off set at 10 percent false alarms on labelled code (set on one half, judged on the other) gives false alarms 0.1086 and misses 0.5002. At the same shared cut-off the other topics miss 0.059 (Education) to 0.437 (Automotive). At four more model readings (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct L13, Llama-3.3-70B L32, Qwen2.5-14B L19, Qwen2.5-72B L32) code scores 0.7951, 0.7841, 0.4963 and 0.5966. The shared cut-off flags 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 and 0.9898 of secure code, and the retuned cut-off misses 0.4802, 0.4100, 0.8701 and 0.9302 of insecure code. The set is not paired (text twin win rate 0.503), so the pairing correction leaves it unchanged. Labels are insecure_code.jsonl (1) and secure_code.jsonl (0) from the paper's release. The paper's own text says misalignment appears when 25 to 75 percent of the mix is malicious, that a 75 percent insecure code mix was needed for mild misalignment, and that insecure code caused less misalignment than every incorrect advice dataset.

Paper text in runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P1086.txt lines 33, 168, 288, 1051 to 1062, 1054, 1132, 1283 and 2532 to 2533.
plain.harm: A team that trusted the 0.963 pooled score to screen fine-tuning data would find that on code the screen either flags all the secure code, so they would have to throw it all away or ignore the alarm, or, once retuned on labelled code, lets about half the insecure code into training, which the paper finds can make a model misbehave on unrelated requests when enough of it is present.
plain.caveat: This is our test, not the paper's. We built a simple difference-of-means direction from the paper's released fine-tuning data and read it on open Llama and Qwen models. The paper proposes a different tool, its own toxic-persona SAE feature on GPT-4o, tracked over a whole dataset. It reports that this feature does rise when 5 percent of a dataset is malicious code. We did not test that tool, so nothing here shows the paper's tool fails. In the paper, insecure code caused less misalignment than any of its bad-advice datasets, and in its mixing test code needed a 75 percent insecure mix to cause mild misalignment. So harm from insecure code that slips past the screen is a risk, not a measured outcome. The code items also differ in kind from the others, since each plants a flaw in code instead of giving bad advice in prose. Even a direction fitted on code alone reads held-out code at only 0.843, so part of the failure is that code is hard for this simple kind of direction, not only that the shared direction misses it. The two Qwen readings sit at about 0.4 of depth. At that depth our depth sweep on truth data found Qwen had not yet formed its shared truth direction. This set was not in that sweep, so those readings carry less weight, and the three Llama readings show the failure without them. The study that set the cut-offs was registered in advance, but this case was picked from its output afterwards. The paper also calls its own study a relatively straightforward auditing scenario, but that remark is about auditing models, not screening data.

The pooled vector, refit with each whole question left out, reads one side's users backwards on 13 of the 17 political questions, and that side is liberal on some questions and conservative on others. A direction fitted on one side mostly picks up which political side the chosen answer takes. plain.headline: At one alarm level, a monitor can miss half or more of a group it ranks well
plain.kind: safety monitor or defense misses a category
plain.paper_says: This is our own case. It tests a common practice, not one paper's claim. The practice is to check a direction group by group with AUROC, the chance that a real case scores above a harmless one, and to take a good score in every group to mean the direction can run as a monitor with one alarm level for every input. P0430 (TRAPSBench) gives the reasoning that makes this look safe when it reports AUROC because the score is threshold-free and so robust to calibration shift.
plain.paper_quote: reporting best-layer AUROC (threshold-free, hence robust to calibration shift)
plain.paper_quote_where: P0430.txt lines 881 to 882, Section 5.4 Probing Internal Representations, just before Table 3 (cross-dataset transfer of the logistic-regression probe). A line break falls between "hence" and "robust", so the quote matches once whitespace is collapsed.
plain.why_wrong: The practice is incomplete, not false. AUROC only asks whether a group's real cases usually score above its own harmless ones. It cannot see where that group's scores sit compared with other groups. If all of a group's scores sit higher or lower than everyone else's, a single shared alarm level lands in the wrong place for that group. In our corpus the practice holds for most well-ranked groups but fails for 159 of the 710. The robustness to calibration shift that P0430 correctly credits to AUROC is exactly why the check cannot show this failure.
plain.evidence: This is our measurement. It is exploratory and unregistered, run as a red-team check at the authors' request. Each direction is fitted with the group left out, and one alarm level is set to flag 10 percent of the other groups' harmless cases. Of 880 groups from 72 datasets, 710 are ranked well (AUROC 0.8 or better). Of those, 159 fail. In 136 the alarm is silent, meaning it misses at least half of the group's real cases. In 23 it is flooded, meaning it goes off on at least half of the group's harmless cases. The silent well-ranked groups have a median AUROC of 0.913, so they are ranked very well. Across all 880 groups, 307 fail. With the group included in the fit, 272 still fail, so leaving the group out is not the cause. A later registered run covered the 689 two-label groups and scored them on split halves, so its baseline is 296 failures, not 307. It shows that for the 525 well-ranked groups the fault is mostly the shared alarm level. Setting each group's alarm level from its own labelled harmless cases, at 10 percent false alarms, cuts their failures from 155 to 20. Resetting it from unlabelled scores cuts them from 155 to 85, about half. Across all 689 groups the unlabelled reset cuts failures only from 296 to 227. That cut of 0.233 fired the registered falsifier, whose bar was 0.25. Even the labelled per-group alarm level leaves 173 groups failing, 168 of them silent.
plain.evidence_where: runs/soundness/corpus72.json threshold.canonical72 (groups 880, well 710, silent 136, flooded 23, all_either_fpr10 307, in_sample_fpr10 272, silent_well_median_auroc 0.9126576171875). SURVEY/paper/CANONICAL.md line 63 (159 of 710, 136 and 23) and line 64 (307 of 880, 272 of 880). SURVEY/data/factsheet.json final claim threshold-flooded-silent (numbers, status exploratory-unregistered, 0.5 bar in caveats, 0.913 median, oracle 155 to 20 run before A06 and not rerun). runs/soundness/recal/corpus.json summary (groups 689, read_well_groups 525, M0 either 296 and either_read_well 155, M2 either 227 and either_read_well 85 and cut_share 0.2331, oracle either 173, silent 168, either_read_well 20). runs/soundness/corpus72.json recal.canonical72 (groups 689, M0_either 296, M2_either 227) and factsheet claim problem1-recalibration caveats (canonical recount reproduces 296 to 227, oracle not rerun). RUNLOG.md line 13332 (red team at the authors' request), line 13386 (10 percent false-positive threshold), lines 13407 to 13427 (registration of the recalibration run and its falsifier), lines 13429 to 13448 (results, falsifier fired at line 13442, reading at lines 13444 to 13448). SURVEY/paper/sections/harm.tex lines 171 to 175, last paragraph of sec:harm-safety.
plain.harm: A team that checked its monitor group by group with AUROC and then ran it at one alarm level would think some groups were covered when the alarm would miss at least half of their real cases, or go off on at least half of their harmless inputs.
plain.caveat: This is exploratory. The threshold check was a red-team analysis run at the authors' request, and it was not registered (RUNLOG.md line 13332). The 880 groups come from 72 datasets that cover many concepts, not only safety. So the case shows what would follow for anyone who deployed such a direction at one alarm level. It is not a documented deployment failure. Silent and flooded use a bar of one half. A silent group therefore misses at least half of its real cases, not necessarily most of them. The current plain sentence in harm.tex says "most", which overstates this, and the authors may want to fix it. The follow-up recalibration run is registered, but it covers only the 689 two-label groups and is scored on split halves. Its per-group figures (155, 85, 20, 173 and 168) come from the run before the grammar-correction recapture (A06) and were not rerun. The recount on the final 72 datasets does reproduce 296 and 227. For the well-ranked groups the fault is mostly the shared alarm level, and resetting it from unlabelled scores fixes about half of that (155 to 85). So saying recalibration does not fix the offsets is too strong for those groups. The falsifier fired on the cut across all 689 groups. Across those 689 groups most failures are a different problem, weak separation inside the group. No per-group alarm level at a 10 percent false-alarm budget fixes that. P0430 is quoted only for the reasoning behind a threshold-free check. It measures transfer with AUROC and does not deploy a monitor at one alarm level, and nothing here shows its own results are wrong.

plain.paper_says: The paper says ordinary jailbreaks do not get past its harmfulness probes. It heads the result "Probes can reliably detect ordinary jailbreaks", concludes that "none of the jailbreaks we test strongly obfuscate activations", and opens its next section by taking as given that existing jailbreak attacks do not bypass harmfulness probes. plain.paper_quote_where: line 385, the first sentence of Section 3.3 Obfuscation Attacks (the narrower sentences it rests on are at lines 365-367 and 375-379)
plain.why_wrong: The claim holds for the paper's stronger probes but fails for the simplest one it tests. That probe is a mean-difference probe, meaning a single "harmfulness" direction found by comparing the model's average internal state on harmful prompts with its average on harmless ones. When it reads only the prompt it catches 0.00 percent of AutoDAN jailbreaks and 0.38 percent of PAIR ones, so for this probe those two attack methods do get past it. The paper qualifies its 90 percent sentence itself, naming the logistic-regression and MLP probes, saying mean difference probes "perform worse" and pointing to Table 1. So the general sentences are incomplete for probes in general and false for this one probe on these two attack types.
plain.evidence: The evidence is the paper's own appendix Table 1, captioned "Jailbreak Detection Performance for Different Probes (Recall @ 1% FPR)". Recall at 1 percent false-positive rate means the alarm is set so that it wrongly flags 1 in 100 harmless prompts, and the number is the share of jailbreaks it then catches. The model is Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The prompt-reading mean-difference probe scores GCG 16.48, PAIR 0.38, AutoDAN 0.00, MSJ (many-shot) 100.00, Multi-Turn 32.99, Prefill 98.98, Misc. 28.75, Average 39.66. The prompt-reading logistic-regression probe scores PAIR 64.02, AutoDAN 100.00, Average 84.48, and the prompt-reading MLP probe scores PAIR 83.33, AutoDAN 100.00, Average 90.35. The same mean-difference probe reading the model's answer instead scores PAIR 23.11, AutoDAN 95.90, Average 71.94. The paper counts only jailbreaks that succeeded, keeping those with a StrongREJECT score above 0.5 and discarding failed attempts.

plain.harm: A deployer who trusted the conclusion that existing jailbreaks do not bypass harmfulness probes, and screened incoming prompts with the simplest probe this paper tests, would let every AutoDAN jailbreak and nearly every PAIR jailbreak reach the model with no flag raised.
plain.caveat: The paper states its limit openly. Its 90 percent sentence names only the logistic-regression and MLP probes, it says mean difference probes "perform worse", and it points readers to Table 1. Those two stronger probes catch every AutoDAN jailbreak and most PAIR ones (64.02 and 83.33 percent) when reading the prompt. So the gap belongs to the one-direction probe and not to probes in general, and it contradicts only the paper's broader sentences about jailbreaks not getting past probes. The same one-direction probe reading the model's answer catches 95.90 percent of AutoDAN jailbreaks but still fewer than a quarter of PAIR ones (23.11 percent). All figures are at one alarm setting (1 percent false positives), come from one model, and count only jailbreaks that succeeded. The paper's main contribution is attacks built to fool probes, so this ordinary-jailbreak result is its baseline and not its headline. This is a harm that would follow for anyone who trusted the general sentence. It is not a reported incident.
